blocks.text: Products disappearing from shelves, reformulations without warning and prices rising unpredictably have become regular occurrences.
Consumers now actively manage their exposure to these disruptions, scrutinising what they buy and demanding complete reliability from their choices.

Value is evolving into confidence that the products and services people rely on today won’t let them down tomorrow, in quality, cost or availability. Brands should make dependability a core part of value propositions.
Ali Angus Head of Innovation

slides.title: From best deal to safe bet

blocks.text: From best deal to safe bet
Cost pressures, supply shocks and service failures have stopped feeling temporary. Instability is now part of daily life.

72% of consumers worry about rising prices of everyday items, a concern that deepens with age.¹ And more than half only buy from brands they trust¹—trust made fragile by stock shortages, reformulations, shrinking packs and tech outages. The result: availability anxiety.
In 2027, the meaning of value expands into a broader question: can I count on this to still be available, work the same and cost what I expect next month, or even years from now?

Consumers expect long-term support in these instances, and changing features or interfaces without warning, even when beneficial, could cause unnecessary friction.

slides.title: Shelf Assured: Regional implications

blocks.text: North America North America is one region where businesses are moving faster than shoppers.

Consumer caution is relatively subdued; around half only buy from trusted brands and research products in detail.⁶ But businesses aren’t taking any chances, with professionals reporting high rates of supply diversification and risk monitoring (42% and 36%, respectively) at their organisations.⁷

Building on COVID-19-era lessons, companies that restructured supply chains then are better equipped to navigate Trump’s tariffs now—from absorbing costs to securing continuity of supply at the right price through diversified suppliers.

North American businesses still face struggling demand, wavering consumer trust and affordability concerns. And engineered reliance raises the stakes—a reminder that the deeper you embed a brand into someone's routine, the less room for error.

Latin America Latin America is where consumers really can’t afford disruption. These consumers are among the most anxious about rising prices (73%)⁸ while also having limited buffers; savings are projected at 9% of disposable income in 2027, well below the global forecast of 15%.⁹

Businesses are responding. 63% of professionals said their company cut costs through operational efficiency, and 55% have already renegotiated supplier or partner contracts, the strongest response of any region. But only 20% enhanced supply chain risk monitoring, the lowest anywhere.¹⁰ Infrastructure explains part of the gap: gross fixed capital formation is expected to account for just 18% of GDP in 2027, down from 20% in 2022,¹¹ and logistics remain fragmented.
Companies can’t diversify supply fast enough to match consumer needs, so a single stockout doesn't just lose a sale but shifts a shopper to a competing brand that proves more reliable.

Middle East and Africa The Middle East and Africa region sits at the intersection of global trade disruption. The Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz made supply volatility a daily reality for these consumers. The region has a young, digitally connected population that demands reliability.
Businesses had to quickly diversify supply, turning continuity into a commercial race and making dependability a precondition for brand competitiveness.

Consumers are drawing boundaries around AI, from its outputs to its societal impact.

People want tools that automate routine tasks, simplify complex choices and streamline decision-making. But they’re wary of privacy risks, misinformation, opaque systems, environmental costs and loss of agency.
As AI becomes ambient and harder to avoid, a new tension emerges where the tech is increasingly useful in daily life but still a source of friction.

For businesses, the signal is clear: adoption depends less on how much the tech can do and more on whether consumers feel confident and comfortable using AI. The winners will be those that make AI useful, transparent and easy to control, with distinct lines between assistance and autonomy.

AI use continues to climb across work, school, shopping and everyday decision-making. 81% of consumers turn to GenAI to assist with daily activities.¹

But adoption doesn’t equal comfort. Concerns around privacy, misinformation, the speed of development and loss of human oversight have led to growing scrutiny of AI’s expanding influence. Only 19% of consumers consider GenAI an extremely trustworthy source of information when shopping,¹² dropping to 12% for health advice.¹³
People are adapting to a system they can’t avoid as AI becomes ambient, creating a new tension where the tech is embedded across touchpoints but still a source of friction at times.

slides.title: Assistance, not autonomy

blocks.text: Assistance, not autonomy

Consumers are learning to rely on AI but want clearer limits on that reliance. The commercial potential of AI is strongest when it facilitates everyday choices: what people buy, how they manage money, which services they use, what information they surface and when they seek human support.

These tools create value when they explain, compare, simplify or help people make more informed choices. Businesses should focus less on automating every interaction and more on making AI feel useful, transparent and easy to control.

Implementing GenAI is already near the top of corporate agendas. More than half of professionals expect GenAI to impact their business within five years, ranking second only to AI overall.¹⁹ But the next phase of adoption is moving closer to purchase execution, and the trust stakes are higher.

Among professionals, 58% expected GenAI to impact their business over the past year by analysing customer data to create more intelligent shopping suggestions.²⁰ Companies need to decide where AI adds confidence, threatens trust or restraint forms part of the value proposition. Smart recommendations reduce effort, but opaque ones quickly come across as intrusive or manipulative.

slides.title: Reluctant Reliance: Regional implications

blocks.text: North America North America is where this trend is most commercially visible. Consumers use AI to simplify decisions, but broader trust remains fragile.

In the US, concern about AI’s societal impact is especially pronounced, creating a sharper divide between practical adoption and emotional comfort. At the same time, the region is already a major testing ground for AI-enabled commerce: the US accounted for 21% of global AI referrals during the first six months of 2026,²² with retailers like Walmart and Amazon pushing AI shopping assistants.

The opportunity is significant, but so is the risk. Brands that make AI useful, explainable and easy to override will gain efficiency and visibility, while those that move too quickly into autonomy may trigger backlash.
Asia Pacific Scale, digital intensity and sharp market variation shape this trend in Asia Pacific.

India and China are already among the leading markets for consumers who’ve purchased through a GenAI platform, but they signal different paths to AI commerce. India highlights the opportunity in open, mobile-first ecosystems where AI can influence discovery and referrals across the web, while China shows how AI-enabled commerce can scale inside closed platform ecosystems where discovery, payment and fulfilment are tightly integrated.
Elsewhere, lower referral shares in markets such as Japan and South Korea show how platform structure, trust and shopping habits can slow AI’s role in the path to purchase.
The regional opportunity is to embed AI into familiar digital routines while keeping its role visible, limited and easy to control.

Western Europe In Western Europe, trust, regulation and control drive this trend. Consumers experiment with GenAI, but stronger expectations around transparency mean adoption is more likely to advance through guided assistance than full autonomy.

Across Europe, 16% of consumers rely on GenAI as a source of information when shopping, up six percentage points in one year,²³ underscoring how quickly AI is moving into discovery without yet becoming the default route to transaction.

AI is already substituting traditional search in the shopping journey; yet GDPR, the EU AI Act, market fragmentation and cautious consumer attitudes slow the shift from recommendation to transaction. As a result, retailers such as Tesco and Carrefour are testing different models that keep control over data, checkout and trust.

As traditional support systems weaken, communities serve as the alternative: a self-selected space that provides the validation and acceptance people struggle to find elsewhere.

slides.title: Peer Powered: Regional implications

blocks.text: Eastern Europe In Eastern Europe, community leans practical and is treated as a source of support or resources rather than identity. Tighter budgets shape this—73% of consumers worry about rising everyday costs²⁸—so people join to gain something tangible. Status or self-expression matter less than whether the group delivers real value.

Belonging here is functional—a way to save money and get by, not to broadcast who you are. The commercial implication is to lead with utility. Brands win in Eastern Europe by making the community demonstrably useful, with identity following rather than leading.
Latin America Trust in national government is low across Latin America, weakened by persistent corruption in its largest markets and a widespread sense that institutions are failing to deliver.

When formal systems command little confidence, people turn to personal networks instead. 50% of consumers said being active in a community is important, among the highest globally.⁸ And 46% consider recommendations from friends and family extremely trustworthy when shopping, well above the roughly 30% average seen elsewhere.²⁹

These personal networks are a key route to discovery and purchase. For brands, that means working with the communities that already exist and showing up where people typically gather. Shared meals and social occasions are a particularly natural fit, creating opportunities to deepen engagement within trusted circles and, ultimately, drive repeat purchase.

Asia Pacific In Asia Pacific, ageing populations and high housing costs are keeping generations under the same roof. That dynamic reinforces family as the foundation of community, where time spent with parents remains highly valued, and gives the Peer Powered trend a natural multigenerational base.
Here, the practical benefits of buying together to save money or get a better deal complement existing habits of participation, shared decision-making and doing things as a group.

Strong participation cultures also give brands an opportunity to involve consumers more directly. 45% of consumers in Asia Pacific want to engage with brands to influence product innovation,³⁰ above the global average. Brands can build on this by adding group-buying features such as bulk discounts, shared shipping or collective purchase thresholds, making it easier for communities to buy together, unlock better value and return for future purchases.

blocks.text: The counterweight behind this Mode-Switching trend emerges when “unmaxxing” or “selective maxxing” becomes part of the equation.
People aren’t abandoning optimisation entirely. But the definition of success shifts towards joy, connection, meaning and quality of life alongside performance, productivity or social validation.
Someone might meal prep, follow a strict workout routine or budget carefully, then happily throw caution to the wind for a special dinner, weekend getaway or impulse purchase.

For others, this takes the form of low-effort activities or solo travelling, where stepping back is a means of restoration, reflection and self-discovery. This signals a future where consumers want the benefits of optimisation, while applying the same intentionality towards inner expressions and who they are, not just outer manifestations and how they appear.
People are discerning about where optimisation merits investment and where presence, purpose and authentic self-expression are sufficient.

blocks.text: With personal success defined by varied outcomes rather than one singular aspiration, solutions that save time, simplify routines or improve daily efficiency should demonstrate the same credibility as those promising health or appearance benefits. Brands also face greater scrutiny when optimisation feels performative rather than meaningful, making authenticity and purpose both critical differentiators.

The strongest propositions help consumers flip seamlessly between modes. Health products that feel like treats, premium experiences without complexity and convenience for low-energy moments all bridge competing priorities without forcing trade-offs.
Brands must therefore help consumers optimise selectively. Those that continue to target fixed identities rather than evolving motivations or shifting need states will be most exposed.

slides.title: Mode-Switching: Regional implications

blocks.text: Middle East and Africa The Middle East and Africa region presents one of the most promising markets for this Mode-Switching trend, driven by a young, aspirational population that associates self-improvement with status and wellbeing.

Consumers in this region demonstrate the strongest appetite for optimisation globally, with 84% tracking at least one health metric⁴¹ and 92% using GenAI to assist with daily activities,⁴² reflecting notable demand for tools that enhance performance and productivity.

Established cultural and religious practices also create natural cycles of discipline, celebration and social connection, making movement between different modes of behaviour feel less contradictory than in other regions.

Commercially, the opportunity extends beyond products into experiential platforms. A clear example is the emergence of longevity clinics in Dubai that position optimisation not as a standalone health pursuit but an integrated lifestyle proposition.
Asia Pacific Asia Pacific demonstrates a more polarised version of this trend.

While optimisation continues to expand through personalised health, beauty and next-gen tech innovations, many people simultaneously prioritise spontaneity and living for the present. These consumers exhibit reward-led behaviours: 93% buy themselves small treats and 19% often make impulse purchases.³⁰

In Southeast Asia, indulgence and escapism remain powerful motivations as people navigate rising living costs while benefiting from dynamic consumer markets. This creates a distinctive pattern in which consumers selectively optimise areas that deliver clear returns, while actively seeking moments of comfort and pleasure elsewhere.
In Japan, the rise of “guilty consumption”, from oversized comfort foods to decadent snacks, illustrates how reward and self-treating are becoming accepted counterweights to everyday pressures.
Performance propositions shouldn’t come at the expense of enjoyment. Brands should legitimise indulgence as an intentional outcome.

Tomorrow on new terms

The future feels less like a guaranteed reward and more like a bet with unpredictable odds. And traditional milestones such as homeownership and retirement seem out of reach. Three pressures converge in 2027 that sit behind this growing consumer scepticism.

Financial cushions are increasingly threadbare. Only 26% of consumers have money readily available for an unexpected emergency, and one in five hold a retirement savings account.¹ Cohorts raised through crisis after crisis aren’t just budgeting differently; many are reinterrogating the very structural rules of the exercise itself.
Volatility feels embedded, with 38% of consumers thinking the world will be more dangerous within five years.¹ People are also renting for longer and expect to move more often.

And faith in prevailing systems of governance is weakening rapidly, especially among young adults. In the US, 62% of 18- to 29-year-olds hold a favourable view of socialism, and a third said the same of communism.⁴³

This isn’t a single generation’s story. There’s a tendency to view the youngest adults in Gen Z as the epicentre, but 30- to 44-year-olds are expressing as much cynicism as any other age group. This cohort is approaching peak earning and household formation. When the people with the most concrete stake in the future are also openly questioning its traditional promises, that points to a structural shift rather than a temporary life-stage phenomenon.
And while consumer confidence has improved from post-COVID-19 lows, negativity persists and shows signs of becoming entrenched, particularly around the outlook.

blocks.text: On the horizon

The same commercial fault line opens across all three consumer responses. People won’t take brand assertions at face value but will pay for a version of the future they can believe in, value and control.
In this climate, brands can’t afford unfounded promises. Consumers want to see evidence of utility immediately, then proof of performance and adaptation to expanding horizons.

Brands now benefit from an authenticity halo, and that halo covers conduct as well as products. Provide concrete value today to earn the credibility to push longer-term propositions. Brands whose behaviour or practices jar with that perception get less benefit of the doubt because purchasing is a lever for these engaged shoppers. And a majority of consumers only buy from companies and brands they trust.¹

In certain instances, company planning extends further ahead. Among professionals, 51% said long-term potential decides which innovation projects get funded, while just 27% weigh speed of ROI.⁴⁷ This risks misalignment with a consumer base pivoting the opposite way.

slides.title: Future Tense: Regional implications

blocks.text: Western Europe Western Europe is where traditional assumptions ran longest and belief is now weakest. Just 44% of consumers think their investments will hold long-term value and 49% expect a more dangerous world within five years—the lowest and highest rates, respectively, of any region.⁴⁸

The response is subtle rather than radical. Consumers are shying away from irreversible commitments across housing and mobility, for example. Long-stay work-live formats such as Zoku and flexible-serviced apartments such as Bob W stand in for permanent addresses, while car subscriptions such as FINN and SIXT+ replace ownership and multi-year leases.

Mature welfare states under fiscal strain and stretched housing markets mean this region has the most future to lose confidence in. The buyer here is defensive but not yet distressed; proof and flexibility beat aspiration.

Eastern Europe Nowhere is the outlook more heavily discounted than Eastern Europe. Only a third of consumers expect to be better off financially in five years and a similar proportion expect life to get worse,²⁸ the weakest and gloomiest sentiments, respectively, across all regions. At the same time, half said they enjoy life without worrying about planning for the future.²⁸
Disengagement shaped by war in the region and lived memory of systems that failed previously are channelling spend into small, immediate, everyday comforts rather than long commitments.

That climate favours present-forward, impulse spending. Żabka Group has become emblematic of this shift, building its business around convenience and everyday purchases. The retailer recorded double-digit sales growth in 2025⁴⁹ and opened more than 1,300 stores across Poland and Romania that year.⁵⁰

Middle East and Africa Middle East and African consumers are the most optimistic anywhere. 66% expect to be better off financially in five years,⁴² which means that present-focus here often takes the form of celebration and self-investment. Whether this sentiment holds could depend in part on how the ongoing conflict in Iran unfolds.

Spiritual life supplies the long-term anchor that formal institutions provide elsewhere. 71% of consumers said spiritual beliefs are important, the highest of any region.⁴² Governments across the Gulf are investing in entertainment, tourism and live events; the sixth edition of Riyadh Season drew more than 11 million visitors to Saudi Arabia by late December 2025.
In this region, the potential to pitch the future as outright opportunity, rather than something to be hedged against, is greater than any other.

blocks.text: Polymarket is a prediction market platform where people trade on the likelihood of future events, such as elections, sports and economic outcomes.
